I remember first noticing this with FileZilla a while back. With linux we can get it through our packaging tools, but a windows friend of mine needed an FTP client so of course I recommended Filezilla, which (at least at the time) directed you to download it through SourceForge. Ok, pretty standard stuff, but then the interesting bits began...

In clicking the "download" link on the FileZilla page (not one of the fake ass download boxes in the ads which in and of itself is pretty sketchy) I noticed the file wasn't "Filezilla" but something along the lines of "SF_Downloader.exe" (or something similar). Ok, this isn't how I remember it, but at this point I'm still willing to give SF the benefit of the doubt, this could be some new sped-up download protocol or something else innocuous. But once it downloads and runs I see that indeed no, it IMMEDIATELY starts trying to push crapware on me, and not only this it does it in a very deceptive way. I forget what exactly the crapware was, but I remember that it was "opt-out" instead of "opt-in", meaning that if you just kept clicking next to download FileZilla then you were going to pass straight through and it would install it for you by default.

And THAT was the moment I lost all respect for SourceForge. It wasn't long after that that they promised "oh, we'll remove the the fake advert download buttons" (they didn't), and "we'll stop pushing crapware on users who just wanted to get their normal programs" (they haven't), and I'm really disappointed that they have chosen not only to take this route but to lie about it in an attempt to placate their (obviously upset) user base.

tldr: SourceForge has promised to stop being evil for a LONG time but the cake is a lie. PLEASE encourage projects to move elsewhere

It was 2010, when I took a course in Beijing on “Classical Readings in Institutional Economics” for my master’s degree. Ludwig von Mises’s book Liberalism was on the reading list.

...

It is very inspiring that there are more and more academic activities by Austrian scholars and similarly minded people. These activities include translating classical books, organizing seminars and reading groups, and even publishing original works related to Austrian economics. But research by Chinese scholars on Austrian economics is not a totally new phenomenon.

For instance, Böhm-Bawerk’s works were translated into Chinese as early as the 1930s. Hayek also had a few Chinese students when he taught at the London School of Economics, and his disciples brought Austrian economics back to mainland China through Taiwan or Hong Kong.
